voices.name: Mason Hale
voices.text: All trusted friends and the online review I’ve read say the Basic with Ads tier cuts out titles we like, adds frequent ads, and removes download capability. The $6.99 price only saves about $3 compared to our current ad‑free plan, which is far less than the $5 discount I’d need to consider switching. Given my high price sensitivity, need for uninterrupted viewing, and the importance of the full catalog for my documentary nights, I remain opposed to moving to the ad‑supported tier.

voices.name: Martha Delgado
voices.segment: current_service=Netflix on an ad-free plan; exact plan unspecified
voices.text: All three trusted friends—Megan, Marjorie, and Margaret—strongly advised staying with the ad‑free tier, emphasizing that ads, title gaps, and no download option would disrupt our documentary and family movie nights. I value uninterrupted viewing and the ability to download for trips, and price isn’t a major concern for me. Given their consistent recommendations, I’m inclined to keep the current ad‑free Netflix subscription.

voices.name: Eleanor J. Morales
voices.text: Eleanor remains unconvinced after hearing multiple trusted friends (Megan, Miriam, Ethan, Walter) all stress the drawbacks of the ad‑supported tier: frequent ads, missing titles, and loss of download capability. Her personal criteria require at least a $5 monthly saving and no more than 2 minutes of ads per hour—both unmet by the $6.99 plan (ads are 4‑5 minutes per hour). She values uninterrupted, full‑catalog viewing for her documentary habit and is willing to keep the higher‑priced ad‑free plan, which aligns with her low price sensitivity and research‑driven decision style.

voices.name: Markus L. Henderson
voices.text: All trusted friends and online reviews stress that the ad‑supported tier would introduce ads and remove titles we regularly watch, especially documentaries. As a loyalist who values uninterrupted viewing and already pays for an ad‑free plan, I see no compelling benefit in switching. Only a noticeable price hike on the current plan would make me reconsider, but none has occurred.

voices.name: Miriam Ortiz
voices.text: Trusted friends (Megan, Walter, Ethan) all report that the ads and missing titles would ruin our viewing experience, especially for documentaries and trips. The $6.99 tier would save about 30% but at the cost of ads, fewer titles, and no download capability, which outweighs the savings for our family. I remain committed to the ad‑free plan and will continue to monitor for any promotional discounts.

narrative.summary: Adoption rose from zero to 12 % by round 5, a rising trend but still judged weak. The service resonated most with U.S. households already on an ad-free Netflix plan, participants in subscription decisions, and viewers who watch at least one hour per week; the prospect segment showed 10.5 % adoption. The weakest group was the “researcher” decision-style segment (7.7 % adoption). The dominant blocker (48 % of objections) was the combination of ads breaking an uninterrupted experience, missing documentary titles, and loss of offline downloads; other objections cited ad frequency and title gaps. Pricing signals show 52 % willing to pay the $6.99 list price and 80 % willing at the $6.02 revenue-max price, while 16 % are unwilling at any price. Adoption spread entirely through influence—six influenced adopters, 83 % reached via a channel post, with top influencer conversion credits of 1.00, 0.83, 0.61. Confidence is wide (CI 0 %–28 %).
recommendations: Deploy a targeted FAQ or short video that directly addresses the top objection—ads breaking an uninterrupted experience, missing titles, and loss of offline downloads—and distribute it through the influencer channel that already reached 83 % of influenced adopters.

Send a personalized email or in-app notification to the 13 respondents identified as the “researcher” decision-style segment, highlighting detailed ad-frequency information and offline-download alternatives to reduce friction for this weakest group.

Center all marketing assets on the $6.99 list price, noting that 52 % are willing at that price, and run a parallel test emphasizing the $6.02 revenue-max price where 80 % are willing, while monitoring the 16 % of respondents who are unwilling at any price.
